summary: A 1976 note on out-of-band control signals in a host-to-host protocol, meaning urgent signals that travel separately from the main stream of data. It is historic and was obsoleted by RFC 7805.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 721 examines how a host-to-host protocol could deliver urgent interrupts reliably without making them wait for ordinary data flow control. It explains the need for a separate interrupt channel and sequence numbers.

questions: urgent data in host to host protocol
what is an out-of-band control signal
why does rfc 721 propose a separate interrupt channel
subtitle: Requirements and design implications for reliable out-of-band interrupts in TCP.

tldr.problem: TCP carries interrupts on the same logical channel as data, so flow control and the need to flush data complicate reliable interrupt delivery.
tldr.mechanism: The memo identifies requirements for a reliable interrupt and explains why a separate interrupt channel and sequence-number space are needed.
tldr.outcome: RFC 721 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 7805.

facts.label: Interrupt delivery requirement
facts.value: Exactly one interrupt per interrupt sent

sections.title: Why Out-of-Band Interrupts Are Difficult
sections.content:
The memo addresses reliable out-of-band control signals, called interrupts. It says TCP handles data and controls on one logical channel. Because interrupts share that channel with data, TCP must flush data when sending an interrupt so that flow control does not block it.

The ARPANET host-to-host protocol separates interrupt and data channels, but the RFC notes that this protocol does not provide reliable transmission of data or controls.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP sends data and interrupts through the same channel. The memo explains how this can make urgent signals depend on data flow control.

sections.title: Requirements for an Interrupt
sections.content:
The sender should be assured that exactly one interrupt reaches the destination for each interrupt sent. The interrupt must be independent of data flow control and should not interfere with reliable delivery of other data and controls.

The host-to-host protocol does not need to synchronize the interrupt channel with the data-control channel. The memo says the user can mark the data stream when generating an interrupt and handle synchronization there.
sections.plainLanguage: Each sent interrupt should arrive once, even when data flow control would block ordinary data. The application can handle synchronization between the interrupt and data stream.

sections.title: Separate Channels and Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
Reliable delivery and accountability require acknowledgments, and sequence numbers can identify interrupts. The RFC says a separate interrupt channel and separate sequence-number space are needed; sharing a sequence-number space could make sending an interrupt wait for resynchronization on another channel.

For multiple channels, the memo discusses using each channel's own sequence-number mechanism or coupling additional channels to channel zero's sequence numbers. It notes that a completely reliable separate TCP interrupt channel requires a full sequence-number space, and describes complications when interrupts are generated rapidly.
sections.plainLanguage: A separate channel keeps interrupts independent of data flow control. Sequence numbers identify interrupts and help detect duplicates, but managing multiple channels creates additional complexity.
